analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and their spouses from owning or trading individual stocks, commodities, and derivatives while in office.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2025 with one cosponsor, the bill has sat in the House Administration Committee without a hearing or vote ever since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would forbid members of Congress and their spouses from holding, buying, or selling individual stocks, stock futures, commodities, or derivatives during the member's term. Members would have 180 days to sell off any prohibited holdings, would have to give up any profits from trades made in violation, and could face repeated fines equal to 10% of the value of anything they refused to divest. Broadly diversified mutual funds, diversified exchange-traded funds, and U.S. Treasury securities would remain allowed.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want lawmakers deciding policy without personal positions in the companies those decisions move. The bill would remove the current setup in which a member can trade stocks in industries they regulate or legislate on, while leaving a paper trail through published annual compliance certifications and a government audit.

how_it_helps.text: Bans members and their spouses from holding, purchasing, or selling any individual security, security future, commodity, or synthetic equivalent (such as options or warrants) during the member's term of service.
Requires members to divest prohibited holdings within 180 days of the law taking effect, or within 180 days of taking office for future members.

Forces members to return any profit from a prohibited trade to the U.S. Treasury and authorizes civil fines equal to 10% of the value of each non-divested instrument, repeating every 30 days while the violation continues.

Requires every member to certify compliance annually, publishes each certification on a public website, and orders the Government Accountability Office to audit member compliance within two years of enactment.
Carves out diversified mutual funds, diversified exchange-traded funds, Treasury securities, and a spouse's pay from their own job, so members can still invest broadly and spouses can keep working.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress who hold individual stocks, commodities, or derivatives, and their spouses, who would have to sell within 180 days and move the money into diversified funds or Treasuries. Wealthy members with large individual portfolios bear the largest adjustment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress holding individual stocks

drawbacks.text: Enforcement is left to the House and Senate ethics committees, and a fined member can appeal the fine directly to a vote of their own chamber as a privileged motion, so the people covered by the ban also control how it is enforced.

A spouse's compensation from their own occupation is excluded, which a good-faith critic could point to as a channel through which a member's household still earns from a spouse's financial-industry career even while the member is restricted.

Members who currently hold large individual portfolios face a forced sale within 180 days, and even supporters acknowledge the rule reaches into family finances well beyond the member's own accounts by covering spouses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but indirect: it does not put money in anyone's pocket directly, it removes a conflict of interest at the center of lawmaking and adds public paper trail and an audit. The costs fall almost entirely on the small group of officeholders covered, and the design's genuine weakness is that it relies on ethics committees made up of the very members it polices, with a built-in appeal to the member's own colleagues. A cleaner bill would use an independent enforcer.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Administration Committee in May 2025 and has had no hearing, markup, or vote since; it sits in committee while Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Alford introduced the bill in the House on May 14, 2025.
It was referred the same day to the Committee on House Administration, the committee that would handle member-conduct rules.
One House Republican cosponsored the bill.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action has been scheduled since referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress who hold or trade individual stocks are better off so far, because the restrictions have never advanced past committee and no vote has been scheduled.

for.name: Rep. Mark Alford
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.role: U.S. Senator (MO), lead sponsor of the Senate companion PELOSI Act
for.what_they_did: Has led the companion version of the PELOSI Act in the Senate, keeping the proposal alive on that side of the Capitol.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for member-conduct rules
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral: no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled in the months since the bill arrived.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and its single cosponsor are both Republicans, and the Senate companion was led by a Republican, while stock-trading bans have drawn interest from both parties in past Congresses, so no party-line pattern is visible in this record.

industries.industry: Members of Congress with individual stock, commodity, or derivative holdings
industries.note: The bill would force these officeholders to divest within 180 days and would fine them 10% of the value of anything they kept, repeating every 30 days. Their interest in continuing to trade while legislating runs against the public interest in lawmakers without personal stakes in the rules they write.

industries.industry: Spouses of members of Congress who actively trade securities
industries.note: The ban covers spouses, though a spouse keeps pay from their own job. This closes the main workaround families have used to keep trading in the member's name.

industries.industry: Diversified mutual fund and ETF providers
industries.note: Members forced out of individual stocks would channel money into broadly diversified funds and Treasuries, the only investments the bill allows. This is a modest, incidental gain, not the bill's purpose.

analysis.trajectory: With one cosponsor and no committee action since May 2025, the bill is unlikely to move this session. Stock-trading ban proposals in recent Congresses have typically died in committee without a floor vote, and this one has shown none of the leadership commitment or committee scheduling that would change that.
